crossref.title: Sequentially Valid Uncertainty: A Bound on Coverage Degradation for Dropout-Informed Conformal Prediction under Regime Shift
crossref.abstract: Monte Carlo (MC) dropout turned an existing regularization trick into a cheap way to get predictive uncertainty from any dropout-trained network, but its uncertainty estimates carry no coverage guarantee and are known to be systematically miscalibrated, particularly under distribution shift. Conformal prediction supplies the missing guarantee, but the classical guarantee requires exchangeable data-an assumption time series violate by construction. Recent work (MC-CP, EPICSCORE, DCP) has begun fusing dropout-derived uncertainty with conformal calibration for sequential data, but treats the fusion as an algorithmic design choice, targeting approximate marginal coverage empirically without a provable account of how the coverage gap scales with the severity of the exchangeability violation. We provide that account. We studentize the conformal nonconformity score by the MC-dropout predictive standard deviation, wrap it in an ACI-style online quantile tracker (DS-ACP), and prove three results: the resulting long-run coverage guarantee is scoreagnostic-inherited from ACI itself rather than a new property of studentization (Lemma 1); an explicit, non-fitted worst-case bound on the finite-time coverage gap via a local exchangeability-violation coefficient δ t (Proposition 1), confirmed in a controlled synthetic experiment where the measured gap correlates with δ t at r = 0.98 (R 2 = 0.96); and a generalization of that bound to arbitrary (not just piecewise-constant) dropout bias via a triangle-inequality argument over pairwise rescaling distances, requiring no linearization and verified numerically in 30/30 randomized configurations (Proposition 2). The paper's distinctive contribution is this diagnostic account of why and by how much dropout-informed conformal scores can fail-not a claim that studentization reliably improves interval efficiency in practice, which we test directly and do not find: on a real trained network, naive MC-dropout variance initially made DS-ACP worse than a raw-residual baseline, traced to a missing aleatoric-variance term and fixed with a held-out variance-floor estimate; but on real electricity and M4 hourly benchmarks (15 series each, two datasets unrelated in domain and scale), an apparent width-efficiency advantage that replicated across seeds for one client did not survive extension to more series, and the same null result replicated independently on the second dataset. We report this retraction directly rather than let the earlier, more favorable result stand. We further run the official code of a real competing system (EPICSCORE) as a baseline; an initial comparison was confounded by a mismatched point predictor, and correcting for it substantially narrows the apparent gap while a smaller, real effect remains. Code, data-access instructions, and full experimental logs for every reported result are released in the supplementary material. Preprint. Under review.

Stokes Shift Prediction of Fluorescent Organic Dyes Using Machine Learning Regression Techniques
crossref.abstract: Fluorescent organic dyes are extensively used in OLEDs, optoelectronics, sensing, light harvesting, dye-sensitized solar cells, and biomedical imaging applications. Scientists have made numerous attempts to synthesize such dyes with the desirable Stokes shift while spending little time and money. To quickly and accurately estimate the Stokes shift of dyes before the experiment, we proposed 15 regression models. In order to achieve the goal, we took into account a dataset of 3066 fluorescent organic materials and used the coefficient of determination (R2), mean absolute error (MAE), and root mean squared error (RMSE) to assess each model's performance. Based on the test scores, the Quadratic Support Vector Machine (QSVM) performed best for Stokes shift prediction, with R2 of 80.40%, RMSE of 24.83 nm, and MAE of 17.28 nm. The experimental data of three Coumarin dyes (Coumarin 30, Coumarin 2, and Coumarin 307) was used to validate the prediction performance of all the investigated models. In this regard, the Medium Gaussian Support Vector Machine (MGSVM) model was the best performer, with errors ranging from 6.04 to 13.53 nm for three Coumarin dyes. The resulting relative errors are substantially less than the recently reported synthesized material relative error of 30 nm. The proposed frameworks enable quick, accurate, and cost-effective screening of a large variety of fluorescent organic dyes, which helps the researchers learn more about the materials beforehand and speeds up the discovery of new compounds.

crossref.title: Multi-Domain Adaptation for Regression Under Conditional Distribution Shift ⋆
crossref.abstract: Domain adaptation (DA) methods facilitate cross-domain learning by minimizing the marginal or conditional distribution shift between domains. However, the conditional distribution shift is not well addressed by existing DA techniques for the cross-domain regression learning task. In this paper, we propose \textit{Multi-Domain Adaptation for Regression under Conditional shift} (DARC) method.  DARC constructs a shared feature space such that linear regression on top of that space generalizes to all domains.In other words, DARC aligns different domains and makes explicit the task-related information encoded in the values of the dependent variable.It is achieved using a novel  Pairwise Similarity Preserver   (PSP) loss function. PSP incentivizes the differences between the outcomes of any two samples, regardless of their domain(s), to match the distance between these samples in the constructed space. We perform experiments in both two-domain and multi-domain settings. The two-domain setting is helpful, especially when one domain contains few available labeled samples and can benefit from adaptation to a domain with many labeled samples. The multi-domain setting allows several domains, each with limited data, to be adapted collectively; thus, multiple domains compensate for each other&apos;s lack of data. The results from all the experiments conducted both on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of DARC.

Regression Conformal Prediction with Nearest Neighbours
crossref.abstract: In this paper we apply Conformal Prediction (CP) to the k-Nearest Neighbours Regression (k-NNR) algorithm and propose ways of extending the typical nonconformity measure used for regression so far. Unlike traditional regression methods which produce point predictions, Conformal Predictors output predictive regions that satisfy a given confidence level. The regions produced by any Conformal Predictor are automatically valid, however their tightness and therefore usefulness depends on the nonconformity measure used by each CP. In effect a nonconformity measure evaluates how strange a given example is compared to a set of other examples based on some traditional machine learning algorithm. We define six novel nonconformity measures based on the k-Nearest Neighbours Regression algorithm and develop the corresponding CPs following both the original (transductive) and the inductive CP approaches. A comparison of the predictive regions produced by our measures with those of the typical regression measure suggests that a major improvement in terms of predictive region tightness is achieved by the new measures.
